To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mRDT and microscopic diagnosis of malaria in school children were less accurate than expected in a district of moderate malaria transmission in Eastern Tanzania.
the sensitivity and specificity were 75.90% and 96.90% for mRDT, and 63.80% and 95.70% for microscopy respectively, when using PCR as the reference standard.
mRDT and microscopic diagnosis have low sensitivity in the detection of malaria infection in primary school children in an area with moderate malaria transmission.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of malaria rapid diagnostic tests (mRDTs) and microscopy for the diagnosis of P. faliparum infection in a primary school in Kibiti, Tanzania.
the development of an effective and reliable method for the diagnosis of malaria infection, and the development of a new diagnostic tool based on PCR.

the evaluation of the diagnostic performance of the HRP II/ pLDH-based mRDT and light microscopy compared with real-time PCR for the diagnosis of P. faliiparum infection among primary schoolchildren in Tanzania.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mRDT and light microscopy have a low sensitivity for detection of low parasitemia and therefore PCR should be used as a gold standard for malaria diagnosis in epidemiological surveys.
the sensitivity of the mRDT was higher than that of microscopy, but the specificity of both was high.
PCR detected more cases than mRDT and microscopic examination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PCR is the best method for detecting malaria parasites.
the diagnostic performance of mRDT and microscopic diagnosis of malaria is suboptimal in areas where transmission intensity is moderate.
mRDT and microscopic examination have low sensitivity and high specificity for detection of low-density P. falciparium infections in Kibiti.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mRDTs and microscopy may not be sufficient to detect all P. falciparium infections in an area with moderate malaria transmission.
the performance of mRDT and microscopic methods for malaria diagnosis is not satisfactory in areas of moderate transmission.
